webTitle: Trump announces new US oil agreement with Venezuela

fields.headline: Trump announces new US oil agreement with Venezuela
fields.trailText: US president says US will have ‘majority’ control of 65bn barrels of proven oil reserves
fields.bodyText: Donald Trump announced Friday a new US oil agreement with Venezuela’s interim president Delcy Rodríguez, saying the US will have “majority” control of 65bn barrels of proven oil reserves. The terms of the agreement remain to be seen, but the US president said on his social-media platform that it had been brokered “through a partnership with ⁠private business” by his secretary of state, Marco Rubio, and defense secretary, Pete Hegseth. The administration, Trump wrote, has “secured majority U.S. control of more than 65 BILLION ‌BARRELS of proven Oil ‌Reserves in Venezuela, at no cost to the ‌American Taxpayer”. Trump said the agreement would more than double American oil reserves. “This deal is a huge win for both the American and Venezuelan people,” Rubio wrote on social media. Trump’s announcement provided few details on the structure of the agreement, the fields or companies involved, or how the US would exercise majority control over the ⁠reserves. Venezuela has an estimated 303bn barrels of proven oil reserves, the world’s largest. Since the US captured and removed former Venezuelan president Nicolás Maduro from power in January, Washington has been trying ‌to secure a stable flow of Venezuelan crude oil for US refineries while promoting American investment into the Opec country’s deteriorated energy industry, which produces 1.25m barrels per day of crude. Trump is under pressure before November’s midterm elections over rising gasoline prices, which could be eased through cheaper oil supplies and expanded output. The US also has ‌been looking for solutions to replenish its strategic petroleum reserve, the oil stockpile, including the possibility of crude swaps with US producers. Earlier this week, the Wall Street Journal reported that the Trump administration was “in advanced talks with Venezuela for the U.S. to take a direct stake in more than a dozen oilfields that house nearly one-third of the country’s massive energy reserves”. Axios also reported on the negotiations, quoting a US official who claimed the deal would be “massive”. The discussion was reportedly over a US stake in Venezuela’s most promising oil-and-gasfields, with some 90bn barrels of proven reserves. The reports caused unease and anger among members of Venezuela’s opposition, who are already up in arms about Trump’s failure to bring about genuine political change after capturing Maduro. “It’s a land grab – a massive land grab,” said one well-known opposition figure who asked not to be named because of the sensitivities of criticizing the US. “It’s revolting because this is not the United States one would have [expected]. This is not the United States of the Marshall plan. This is a rapacious, mafioso United States.” The announcement comes as Chevron and other US energy companies are expected to sign a deal next week investing billions in Venezuela’s oil fields, according to the Journal. Tom Phillips and Reuters contributed reporting

webTitle: Labour rejects Zack Polanski’s call to ‘slam brakes’ on building AI datacentres

fields.headline: Labour rejects Zack Polanski’s call to ‘slam brakes’ on building AI datacentres
fields.trailText: Government says Green leader’s proposed moratorium on ‘energy-guzzling’ AI projects would be disaster for economy
fields.bodyText: Labour has rejected calls to pause construction of major AI infrastructure in Britain after the Green party leader, Zack Polanski, said it was time to “slam the brakes on these energy-guzzling, water-guzzling datacentres”. The government hit back at the opposition party’s proposal of a “moratorium other than [for] local-scale datacentres for the local community”, saying it “would be a disaster for jobs and national security”. The Greens’ call for a pause comes amid one of the UK’s worst droughts in years and predictions that datacentres’ electricity use, now standing at about 2.5% of the UK’s supply, will rise fourfold by 2030. Datacentres contain the processing chips that power billions of AI prompts every day and Labour has designated them as critical national infrastructure, a decision Polanski called “outrageous”. “To most people critical infrastructure means hospitals, water, electricity,” he said. “It doesn’t mean artificial intelligence.” He added: “Right now the government is putting our communities, our water security and our climate ambitions second to the demands of tech giants.” A spokesperson for the government said: “A pause on building new datacentres would simply send investment and good jobs abroad, while leaving Britain dependent on overseas computing for the processing of sensitive health and defence data.” They said critical national infrastructure status did not give datacentres priority access to water or electricity, nor did it automatically put them ahead of households during shortages, and that in England datacentres’ water usage represented less than 1% of non-household water consumption. The row comes amid increasing signs that datacentre policy, already a major political issue in the US midterm elections, is rising up the agenda in Britain. In energy- and water-rich Scotland, the Scottish National party government appears to be “inching towards a moratorium” amid voter pressure, while local disputes have erupted from Devon to Buckinghamshire and Cardiff to Fife where residents have raised fears about noise, heat, traffic and the visual impact of datacentres affecting house prices. The AI minister, Kanishka Narayan, has linked the need for more AI datacentres to strong defence and this month claimed the British public “doesn’t just want foreign billionaires to own things that matter to our lives. If we’re being true to those British values, it is impossible to achieve that without building a sovereign level of datacentre capacity.” The government spokesperson said its refusal to pause development “does not mean a blank cheque for big tech or that every datacentre should be approved”. They said developers should “prioritise clean power, use water responsibly, create British jobs and supply chains, and provide investment to the communities in which they are built”. The tech equity campaign group Foxglove warned that with some datacentre developers seeking to mitigate long waits to connect to the energy grid by planning their own gas-fired power stations, there was a risk of a “deeply alarming backward step on climate action”. Rosa Curling, its co-executive director, said: “It’s good to hear that the government thinks there shouldn’t be a ‘blank cheque’ for big tech’s datacentres. But without urgent action, that’s exactly what will happen – the public and the planet will be left to foot the bill for the environmental and social costs of these energy-hungry giants.”

webTitle: Vaccine misinformation spreads as RFK Jr suggests two measles deaths were ‘fabricated’

fields.headline: Vaccine misinformation spreads as RFK Jr suggests two measles deaths were ‘fabricated’
fields.trailText: Anti-vaxxers are spreading conspiracy theories after two recent measles-associated deaths in Pennsylvania
fields.bodyText: Anti-vaccine activists are trying to track down the families of two people, including at least one newborn, who died after contracting measles in Pennsylvania, as Governor Josh Shapiro tangles with Robert F Kennedy Jr over his “inaccurate and misleading claims”. Kennedy, the secretary of the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), suggested late on Wednesday that the deaths in the state may have been “fabricated” after a Republican coroner – an elected political office in Lancaster county – claimed one of the measles-associated deaths was unrelated to the virus, although the given cause would be consistent with measles. Brian Hooker at Children’s Health Defense, an anti-vaccine organization that until recently was led by Kennedy, said in a recent video that the organization is “trying to get boots on the ground” and “do outreach” in Pennsylvania. Kennedy is “an anti-vaccine activist in the role of the most powerful public health person in this country”, said Paul Offit, an infectious diseases physician at Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia. “It’s like the world’s turned upside down.” It would be helpful to know the deceased patients’ ages and more information about their deaths, he added. “By not having that information, it allows fertile ground for the kind of conspiracy theory that RFK Jr puts out there, where he said in some posts that these weren’t measles deaths.” The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) said in a Thursday post on X that it was “working to determine what actually occurred”, including “whether the two reported deaths were caused by measles”. The HHS did not respond to the Guardian’s questions about whether Kennedy recommends the vaccine or whether the newly confirmed CDC director, Erica Schwartz, would make a statement about the outbreak and the need for vaccination. About 424 Pennsylvanians have confirmed measles cases, and 73 have been hospitalized. None of the sickened people are fully vaccinated. The two deaths were in unvaccinated patients in Lancaster county, Pennsylvania, which is home to large Amish and Mennonite communities. While these communities do not have religious objections to vaccines, they eschew many parts of modern life, and thus are relatively disconnected from modern healthcare. Few other details have been released about the patients, fueling a firestorm of misinformation from anti-vaccine activists spreading conspiracy theories about vaccines, which are 97% effective at preventing measles. The anti-vaccine activists are attempting to figure out who died so they can reach the families, as they did in Texas when a six-year-old girl died last year, Hooker said. They filmed a misinformation-filled interview with the Mennonite parents in a rare media appearance after their daughter’s death. Hooker also speculated that the Pennsylvania announcement was a political ploy in advance of the US midterm elections, claiming it was “a strategic move” to “get measles deaths on the tip of everybody’s tongue, to get in the forefront”. The Trump administration has at times attempted to downplay its anti-vaccine moves because they are not popular with voters, according to internal polling. When Shapiro first announced the deaths, he pointed to the inaccurate claims from the highest levels of the US government, saying at a press conference: “There’s real-life consequences to spreading misinformation.” Kennedy responded on X with debunked myths about the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine. Shapiro called those claims “inaccurate and misleading” in his own X post. When Kennedy offered to help after the announcement of the two deaths, Shapiro asked him to encourage vaccination and stop spreading misinformation, the governor said in the post. The health secretary responded by repeating vaccine misinformation and saying “it would be better if we went back to ‘natural measles’,” Shapiro wrote. “Secretary Kennedy has stoked confusion amongst parents and others – and the result has been less protection from measles and more cases,” Shapiro added. In 2021, for instance, Kennedy gave a speech praising Amish parents in Lancaster county for not vaccinating their children. “The cure for measles is chicken soup and vitamin A,” he said. There is no cure for measles, only supportive care. A few hours after Shapiro’s response, Kennedy posted to X wondering whether the deaths had been “fabricated” and alleging that Pennsylvania was refusing to share information with the CDC. But Pennsylvania notified the CDC of the deaths early on Tuesday morning, before making the public announcement, Dr Debra Bogen, the state’s secretary of health, said in a statement. “I have thoroughly reviewed the case investigation information and sadly can confirm that there were two recent measles-associated deaths in Lancaster County,” she said. The cases were also thoroughly investigated by the state’s epidemiology team, and both individuals tested positive for measles, she added. One of the deaths was in a newborn who tested positive for measles, the department of health said on Facebook. Stephen Diamantoni, the coroner for Lancaster county, told the Philadelphia Inquirer that a test on the baby’s lung tissue after death indicated a measles infection acquired before birth. He believes the baby died shortly after birth because of a lacerated spleen. Spleen issues are a known complication of measles infection. Having an enlarged spleen from measles “was not uncommon actually in the pre-vaccine era”, Offit said. The scientific literature includes doctors’ observations of enlarged spleens, which can lead to rupture. “If you have an enlarged spleen and you’re infected with measles virus, the measles virus caused your enlarged spleen. If you then have a splenic rupture which kills you, you die from measles,” Offit said. Anti-vaccine activists have been successful in driving down vaccination rates, Offit said. The ensuing outbreak “isn’t a good look” for them, he said. Children’s Health Defense appeared to want to downplay its role and put out “the same kind of bad information” after the children died in Texas, Offit said. “It’s very easy to convince those parents – very easy – that this wasn’t their fault, because otherwise, they would have to take on the responsibility or the notion that they could have prevented their child’s death.” Hooker complained on Wednesday that the scant details released about the patients made it difficult to reach them. He also noted that his organization was unable to contact the family of a measles-positive adult who died in New Mexico last year, because the state did not release more public information. “The more information that they release regarding these particular deaths, the more that we would be able to dig in and contact family members, get access to medical records and see exactly what happened,” said Hooker. Children’s Health Defense has claimed that one of the child deaths in Texas last year was due to medical error, not measles, despite findings from officials on measles. Measles deaths have become rare in the US because of vaccination, but between one and three people usually die with every 1,000 infections. The US is now experiencing its worst outbreak of measles in three decades. It is unusual for measles to spread in summer months like this – and now children are heading back to school, potentially amplifying transmission, Offit said. “You’re just going to see, I think, an explosion of measles.” Infants under the age of six months are too young to be vaccinated against measles, which is a large reason why it is important to vaccinate pregnant parents and others in the community, Offit said. More than 35,000 Pennsylvanians got vaccinated against measles last month – an increase of 10,000 compared to typical months.

webTitle: Detroit despairs as ‘insanity’ of Trump’s Canada trade war punishes city

fields.headline: Detroit despairs as ‘insanity’ of Trump’s Canada trade war punishes city
fields.trailText: Unpopular new policy comes as midterms loom and control of Congress could be decided by several Michigan races
fields.bodyText: Every day $1bn worth of goods crosses the river dividing Detroit, Michigan, and Windsor, Ontario, two largely blue-collar US and Canadian cities that have come to act as one in the creation of North America’s auto industry. News this week of Donald Trump’s escalating trade spat with Canada has everyone worried. Political and economic leaders and observers labeled the move an act of “hubris” , blamed Trump’s “ego”, and called the escalation “insanity”. “We don’t need Canada, they need us,” Trump declared. But many are hoping that Trump’s imposition of 50% tariffs on Canadian goods this week will not last long, with the upcoming midterm elections as a pivotal reason the plan may be scrapped. Control of the US Congress hangs in the balance and will almost certainly be decided by several close Michigan races. It also comes just two months after polling highlighted Michiganders’ fatigue with and opposition to the president’s unprecedented tariff program. By a 63%-31% margin, residents here oppose tariffs on Canadian goods, according to a June Epic-MRA poll, including 35% of Republicans. Meanwhile, nearly 75% of Michiganders said the tariffs are fueling high prices. Trump doubling down on an unpopular policy deep into election season is viewed by many observers as a gift to Democrats, and there is a real possibility that it contributes to a midterm loss for the Republicans. Meanwhile, there seems to be little upside for Trump. “I don’t understand what Trump is thinking,” the Epic-MRA pollster Bernie Porn said. Regardless, Michiganders have already suffered disproportionately as they pay on average over $3,200 annually for tariffs, or about 142% more than the rest of the country, because of the state’s shared border with Canada. The Canadian economy would also take a major hit if the tariffs are imposed, said Patrick Anderson, a Michigan-based economist with the Anderson Economic Group. “Both will suffer – there are no two ways about it,” Anderson added. This critical upper midwest swing state has picked the presidential winner in five consecutive elections, going from Barack Obama to Trump to Joe Biden and back to Trump. Democrats’ chances to retake the Senate rest heavily on the Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed beating Trump ally Mike Rogers in the 3 November general election race. Rogers has supported the tariffs, but so far has been silent on the latest escalation. The tariffs and the unpopular Iran war’s contribution to inflation represent a “double hit” for Republicans, Porn said, and Trump is handing ammo to a particularly adept candidate in El-Sayed. He has energized people with his anti-establishment, populist political vision, and a no-holds-barred delivery. “El-Sayed has proven to be very, very articulate on a number of issues,” Porn added. “I think that he is going to try and just throw bombs at Rogers [in an upcoming debate] because Rogers supports these tariffs and trade war. Trump’s low popularity is an anchor around Rogers’ neck.” In a statement, El-Sayed hammered Trump and Rogers, saying that the president “cares more about his ego and saber-rattling than addressing the affordability crisis. “Donald Trump is launching this trade war for his own vanity, and he’s asking Michigan families to pay the price,” El-Sayed said. “Trump has been failing Michigan through these chaotic tariffs and bad trade deals for far too long, and Mike Rogers won’t do anything but rubber-stamp them.” El-Sayed said he would push for “real, fair trade deals that create good-paying jobs”. Rogers’ campaign did not respond to a request for comment. The United Auto Workers (UAW), which has 350,000 members in Michigan and is often a political kingmaker here, has supported some of Trump’s targeted tariffs, but said in a statement it “rejects” the latest escalation. “If we’re going to increase tariffs anywhere, it should be on countries where automakers continue to offshore jobs because they can pay workers $3 an hour, force them to work in unsafe conditions, and crack down on independent unions,” the UAW president, Shawn Fain, said. Canada has strong unions, and the UAW supports those. “Tariffs work, but only if they are deployed intentionally to protect workers and grow our manufacturing communities, and it’s time to permanently end offshoring and the race to the bottom,” Fain added. Mexico and Canada currently face 25% US tariffs on autos, though partial exemptions in the nations’ free trade agreement make the effective rate much lower, overall. Anderson estimated tariffs cost US auto companies about $12.5bn in 2025. The Canadian government has announced it will impose retaliatory tariffs on $20bn of goods starting 8 September. The actions leading to the latest blow-up have been “rife with miscalculations, overreactions, and hubris”, Anderson said. He read through the list of goods on which tariffs would be imposed – feathers, sweaters, girls’ dresses, lobster. “This is not a trade war. This is an annoyance list. Chest pounding,” Anderson said. The North American auto industry over the last 60 years has integrated across the continent, and auto parts cross a border an average of six times before they land in a final product. That means there would be shared pain, Anderson said, and it would reverberate across the upper midwest, where bigger manufacturing cities are typically powered by industries that are often reliant on international trade. But the Canadian economy is smaller, and Ontario’s economy is so concentrated that it would hit harder north of the border, Anderson added. Ultimately, the real threat is that “these two countries go pell-mell into it” and impose tariffs on oil, energy and commodities that hit harder than lobster. The dialogue has devolved into the usual petty antagonism that is a hallmark of Trump’s beefs. Trump signed an executive order to rename Lake Ontario “Lake America” on Thursday, and Vice-President JD Vance referred to Canada as the 51st state. “Let me say with great understatement that this is not helpful,” Anderson added. Indeed, the Windsor mayor, Drew Dilkens, took exception to that particular comment. In an interview, he expressed deep frustration over Trump’s moves, and labeled justifications Trump has used for issuing tariffs, including framing them as a response to illegal immigration on the northern border, “nonsense”. The latest escalation “is an aggressive move, one that could not be ignored by our country”, added Dilkens, who leads the city of 230,000 people. “It’s just offensive that he launches these attacks at Canada, who is your largest trading partner, your closest ally, and your neighbor.” The chaos has cooled investment in Windsor, and prices remain high on both sides of the border. He pointed out how much more US consumers are paying not just for automobiles, but for beef, which in part stems from tariffs on Canadian beef. “What is really crazy is that he is willing to throw his own citizens under the bus to pursue his tariff agenda,” Dilkens said. “They have Donald Trump to thank.” Highlighting the tension among the president and some in his base, the Michigan chamber of commerce, a trade organization that lobbies on behalf of the state’s largest corporations, normally vocally supports the president on economic issues. It has not made a public statement, and did not respond to a request for comment from the Guardian. However, the typically pro-Trump Detroit chamber of commerce did not mince words. “Escalating tensions and tariffs will only cause economic pain on both sides of the border, especially in Michigan and the binational Detroit-Windsor region,” the chamber said in a press statement, adding that global competitors like China benefited most. “Our economies are intertwined, interconnected, and stronger together; the sooner normalcy is restored the better.” • This article was amended on 28 August 2026. An earlier version gave incorrect commencement dates for the US and Canadian tariffs.

webTitle: Trump’s midterm campaign theme is unrequited love | Sidney Blumenthal

fields.headline: Trump’s midterm campaign theme is unrequited love
fields.trailText: The president senses a crisis in his cult of personality. He believes the path to victory is through unwavering devotion
fields.bodyText: Donald Trump has framed his theme for the midterm elections. It has come to him as naturally and inevitably as staring into the mirror, beyond any logic or argument, his definitive answer to no specific issue, providing no understanding of any particular problem, but transcending all of them. His political theme is more primal than programmatic, more instinctive than analytical, a heartfelt expression to protect his greatest romantic attachment, his obsessive fixation, his idealized object: himself. Trump’s campaign theme is unrequited love. Unlike the pollsters, media consultants and pundits, he alone has grasped the magnitude and the source of the existential crisis threatening his politics. He has identified the problem for the Republicans as the faltering measure of complete devotion to him. His demand has nothing to do with mutual affection. It is a ploy to reassert his slipping control, a manipulative test to prove loyalty to him, or else. There can be no absolute rule without an absolute ruler; no absolute ruler without absolute submission; no absolute submission without the expression of absolute love. His sadness at its fading gives way to anger, paranoia and greater acts of retribution. He equates the fear he instills as a form of love. Trump accepts subservience, from whatever motive, as affection or its closest equivalent. He cares nothing about sincerity, so it’s all in the show. The less love displayed, the more fear required. Yet there is no rebound, but only deeper rejection. Trump is heading toward the floor for presidential unpopularity – Nixon during Watergate on the eve of his resignation, Truman late in his second term at the depth of the Korean war, and George W Bush at the 2008 financial crash. But Trump’s breakdown differs uniquely from theirs. His decline has come earlier in his term, been more sustained, and his disintegration has not stabilized but is accelerating. He is being crushed by the accumulation of catastrophic events of his own making to which his impulsive response is to double down in each and every area. Stalemated in his reckless Iran war, he has now launched a heedless trade war against Canada that will devastate Republican candidates in the northern tier of states. His latest vanity project is gestural retribution to rename Lake Ontario as “Lake America”, a watery ballroom. Admission of error for Trump would be the denial of self-love. Trump began his campaign on his unrequited love theme on 16 August during a Fox News interview in which he discussed his press secretary, Karoline Leavitt, leaving her job after just having a baby. He had held her up as meeting his highest criterion in remarks last December: “Isn’t she great? Is Karoline great? … She gets up there with that beautiful face and those lips that don’t stop, ba ba ba like a little machine gun.” Now, he tried to make a joke of her departure that expressed resentment at abandonment. “In fact, she likes her children more than she likes Trump. I’m very concerned about that,” he said. Then he repeated his unfunny “joke” at a campaign rally in South Carolina on 21 August: “I just learned she loves the baby more than she loves Donald Trump, and I’m very angry …” Trump’s lame attempt at humor was a rare instance of his truth-telling and self-revelation, a contemporary illustration of Freud’s Jokes and Their Relation to the Unconscious. Trump was in South Carolina to campaign for his chosen candidate in the Republican primary, Darline Graham, who he had insisted be appointed to the Senate seat of her brother Lindsey Graham after he died on 11 July. Darline Graham confessed to cluelessness when asked in a debate about her position on Taiwan. “National security is not my thing,” she answered. “I’m not … that informed on national security.” But she was fully informed on the necessity of obedience to Trump. “You saved our country, and I want to thank you for that,” she said at the rally. Trump praised his worshipper: “She’s got a good gene pool.” She was born to love him. She stood in stark contrast to the immigrants he had described as “poisoning the blood of our country”. Then Trump called on the crowd to embrace his new theme. “So what I really want you to do is pretend, please, that I’m on the ballot … So just say that I’m on the ballot one more time. You got to say it.” He wishes every candidate to sound like Darline Graham in proclaiming him the national savior. He insists he is beloved, and if those who revere him turn out the Republicans must win. In fact, though he is not on the ballot in the midterm elections, Trump is the central issue. Voters do not have to “pretend, please”. Trump intuitively comprehends that the midterm elections are about him in a way that makes this midterm unlike any other. In the marrow of his bones, he senses it is a crisis of his cult of personality. Trump’s Maga was never a new party structure, but constructed on his wreckage of the old Republican party. In its place, every particle of the replacement is connected to the leader to advance his supremacy and self-enrichment. Everything flows upward, all heads tilted, all knees bent. Maga has always been Maga Inc of, by and for one man. The movement is the man. When charisma fails, the movement implodes. If the leader is not worshipped, his uber-principle – the leader principle – collapses: no fuhrerprinzip, no Führer. Trump’s plea for their unconditional love – “pretend, please” – defies gravity. He is running against Isaac Newton, and Newton always prevails. Intensity is gauged by “strongly approve” and “strongly disapprove” poll numbers. More than the general statistics of approval or disapproval, these provide insight into the motivation of voters that determine the contour of elections. Trump now stands at 13% “strongly approve” in the most recent Reuters-Ipsos Poll. His “strongly disapprove” rating is at 49%. His total approval is at 33%, while disapproval is at 65%. Those in the “somewhat approve” category include low propensity soft voters especially inclined to skip midterm elections. And this poll was taken before his declaration of trade war against Canada. All along, the Republicans have been Trump’s indispensable accomplices. Even if they were disposed to object, they could do nothing to draw him back from his “pretend, please” campaign. His anxiety to rescue his invincible image from the reality he’s created makes him more inescapable than ever. Any effort to restrict him will provoke his rage. He will not diminish himself for the sake of the party or even his own future. He plans to spend millions from his Maga Inc political action committee to tell the voters that they have never had it so good – “the greatest economy we’ve ever had, by far”, he says. He has mocked the suggestion that “affordability” might be a problem for many – it’s “a word they”, the media, “devised”, he has said. Trump intends to stage a mini convention in Dallas on 9 September, featuring Donald Trump to “celebrate … our achievements”. Republicans are locked almost uniformly into blind support, with the Maine senator Susan Collins venturing hollow criticism of the Canadian tariffs that makes her seem powerless and infuriates the remaining Maga base. Just as Trump has trapped himself, he has trapped the Republicans. The expenditure of tens of millions to depict his dire consequences as paradise on earth will have the unintended effect of supercharging the already motivated “strongly disapprove” voters and disillusion those who cannot help but be aware of the actual conditions of their own lives. The sudden surfacing of Natalie Harp as a meme at this particular moment propitiously coincides with the wobbling of Trump’s cult. The 35-year-old is his model of the perfect staffer, perfect companion and perfect American citizen. If unrequited love is the problem, she is the solution. In Trump’s hierarchy of need, his pyramid of status, love and self-actualization, she is at the apex. Harp is his “binky”, as Maggie Haberman of the New York Times has called her, his comfort blanket, his plush bunny rabbit. The “human printer” who trails after him, pressing the button to churn out an endless stream of adulatory articles, conspiracy theories and “alternative facts”, has become an extension of his nervous system. The former anchor at the fringe far-right One America News Network serves as Trump’s personal anchor. Harp broadcasts around the clock to an audience of one. She is the connector to the neurons of the far right, serving as a conduit to dodgy characters such as Laura Loomer with her lists of national security officials who were supposedly disloyal. Harp is Trump’s neurotransmitter who distributes a steady supply of dopamine and delusion. Harp’s self-abasing devotion to Trump, expressed in her letters to him, serves as a kind of inadvertent political manifesto for the cult, a template for followers. Harp tellingly muddles a line from Jane Austen’s Pride and Prejudice – Mr Bennet blessing his strong-willed daughter Elizabeth in her engagement to Darcy – to demean herself and offer subservience to Trump: “To modify a classic, ‘I could not have parted with you, to anyone less worthy’ – And, I will add, it is I who is unworthy.” In another letter, after self-disparaging apologies, Harp writes: “You are all that matters to me. I don’t want to ever let you down. Thank you for being my Guardian and Protector in this Life … With all my Heart.” As public opinion curdles on Trump, no longer able to “pretend, please”, Harp has not come to the wisdom of Conway Twitty in his 1959 rockabilly hit: My only prayer will be Someday you’ll care for me But it’s only make believe Sidney Blumenthal, former senior adviser to President Bill Clinton and Hillary Clinton, has published three books of a projected five-volume political life of Abraham Lincoln: A Self-Made Man, Wrestling With His Angel and All the Powers of Earth. He is a Guardian US columnist and co-host of the Court of History podcast

webTitle: Canadian prime minister and New York lawmaker denounce Trump’s move to rename Lake Ontario as Lake America – as it happened

fields.headline: Canadian prime minister and New York lawmaker denounce Trump’s move to rename Lake Ontario as Lake America – as it happened
fields.trailText: This live blog is now closed.
fields.bodyText: This concludes our live coverage of the second Trump administration for the day. Here are the latest developments: Documents obtained by the Guardian and interviews with military leadership show the war in Iran has depleted the US Navy’s budget. A senior Democratic senator is calling for a criminal investigation into the US health secretary, Robert F Kennedy Jr, following reporting by the Guardian that indicated he lied during Senate confirmation hearings last year. Donald Trump called the media into the Oval Office to watch him sign an executive order to rename Lake Ontario “Lake America”. “The name Lake Ontario comes from the Wendat word Ontari’io, which, appropriately, means ‘the lake is beautiful, the lake is big’, Canada’s prime minister Mark Carney noted. “The name is more than 400 years old, predating both the Confederation of Canada and the Declaration of Independence of the United States of America.” Three journalists who were fired by the Pentagon from a US government-funded news outlet sued the US Department of Defense in federal court in Washington DC on Thursday arguing that their dismissals were illegal and violated their First Amendment rights to free speech. Two minutes before Air Force One landed in Houston on Thursday, Donald Trump posted a visual ranking of US presidents on his social media platform that described him as the “greatest” president, in a list that omitted, without explanation, 11 of his predecessors. As critics of the president quickly pointed out, the illustrated ranking of presidents was an altered version of one published in Life magazine on 1 November 1948. The original illustrated an article about the rankings compiled by the Harvard professor Arthur M. Schlesinger Sr. who polled 55 historians, journalists and political scientists and asked them to rate presidents in one of five categories: great, near great, average, below average and failure. In the article published the day before the 1948 election, Schlesinger explained that he had left out three presidents, William Henry Harrison who died after a month in office; James Garfield, who was shot four months after his inauguration; and Harry Truman, who was still serving out the term his predecessor Franklin D Roosevelt had been elected to before his death. The date of the illustration explains why another eight presidents are missing from the list that puts Trump at the top. Dwight Eisenhower, John F Kennedy, Lyndon Johnson, Richard Nixon, Gerald Ford, Ronald Reagan, George H W Bush and George W Bush all, of course, were elected after 1948.
